clinicalPearls: Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous infection of the upper respiratory tract caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis (a subspecies of Klebsiella pneumoniae)
It is endemic in parts of Africa, the Middle East, Central and South America, Asia and Eastern Europe, and is linked to poor hygiene and crowding
Disease evolves through catarrhal, granulomatous (proliferative) and sclerotic (fibrotic) stages over months to years
The granulomatous stage produces the characteristic nodular masses that can deform the nose and obstruct the airway
Histology reveals Mikulicz cells (large vacuolated macrophages containing bacteria) alongside plasma cells with Russell bodies
Prolonged antibiotic therapy is required, using agents such as fluoroquinolones or tetracyclines, guided by susceptibility
Surgery may be needed to relieve airway obstruction or correct deformity in the fibrotic stage
reference.pathophysiology: Rhinoscleroma results from chronic infection of the respiratory mucosa by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, an encapsulated Gram-negative bacillus acquired by inhalation, typically in conditions of overcrowding and poor sanitation. The organism is engulfed by macrophages but resists intracellular killing, giving rise to the distinctive foamy Mikulicz cells that dominate the granulomatous stage. A sustained inflammatory response with plasma cells and Russell bodies leads progressively to fibrosis and scarring. This staged process explains the transition from non-specific catarrhal symptoms through proliferative masses to the sclerotic deformity and airway narrowing of late disease.
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy for histology demonstrating Mikulicz cells and Russell bodies
Culture of tissue for Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis
Special stains (e.g. Warthin-Starry, periodic acid-Schiff) to highlight organisms within macrophages
Nasal endoscopy to assess the extent of masses and airway compromise
Cross-sectional imaging to evaluate deeper and paranasal involvement
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing to guide prolonged therapy
redFlags: Airway obstruction from nasal or laryngeal masses
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring exclusion of malignancy or vasculitis
Extension to the larynx or lower airway
reference.prognosis: With prolonged appropriate antibiotics the infection can be controlled, but late fibrotic disease may leave permanent structural deformity and airway narrowing, and relapse can occur if therapy is inadequate in duration.
pitfalls: Stopping antibiotics too soon, allowing relapse of this indolent infection
Mistaking granulomatous masses for malignancy or vasculitis without biopsy
Failing to recognise Mikulicz cells as the diagnostic histological clue
Neglecting airway assessment in advanced disease
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prolonged antimicrobial therapy directed at Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, using fluoroquinolones or tetracyclines and continued for an extended course to eradicate intracellular organisms and prevent relapse
Culture of tissue with susceptibility testing to guide and, if needed, adjust the antibiotic choice
Endoscopic debulking or surgical resection of obstructing granulomatous masses and correction of sclerotic deformity
Airway management for late fibrotic stenosis, including endoscopic dilatation and tracheostomy where obstruction is severe
Clinical and endoscopic surveillance after treatment to detect relapse from inadequate therapy duration
Address overcrowding and poor sanitation as public-health preventive measures
